---
title: "OMK JSON: format specification"
subtitle: "Draft 0.1 — not yet stable"
---

## Status of this document

This is a **draft** of version 0.1 of the OMK JSON format.
While a vocabulary's version begins with `0.`,
any part of it may change incompatibly (§6.3).

The format is defined by three pages:
this one (the data model, the envelope, the canonical form, and what readers and writers must do),
the [`omk` vocabulary](vocabulary-omk.qmd) (the core types),
and the [`wsmn` vocabulary](vocabulary-wsmn.qmd)
(the types of Western Standard Music Notation).

## 1. Scope

An OMK JSON document holds one OMK graph:
musical objects (*nodes*), the typed relationships between them (*edges*),
and the values the objects are made of (pitches, durations, marks, ...).
It holds the music and the data applications attach to it,
and nothing about any particular implementation:
no database or graph-library identifiers,
no programming-language types or module names.

The format is written so that an implementation of OMK in any language,
using the names and data types defined by the vocabularies,
can read and write the same documents,
and so that a document read and written again comes out byte for byte the same (§9).

## 2. Conventions

The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT,
RECOMMENDED, MAY and OPTIONAL are to be interpreted as described in
[RFC 2119](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2119) and
[RFC 8174](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8174)
when, and only when, they appear in all capitals.

*JSON* is as defined by [RFC 8259](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8259).
A *reader* turns a document into a graph;
a *writer* turns a graph into a document.

## 3. Data model

A **graph** is a set of nodes and a set of directed edges between them,
together with a little metadata about the graph itself.
There may be any number of edges between two nodes,
but at most one edge of a given relation from one node to another (§10).
A graph need not be connected, need not be a complete score,
and need not have a score at all:
sketches, fragments and analyses are graphs too.

A **node** is a musical object: a note, a chord symbol, a key change, a slur, a part, a score.
Every node has a type, an identifier, metadata, and the fields its type defines.
No field of a node refers to another node;
every relationship between nodes is an edge.

An **edge** is a relationship from one node (its *source*) to another (its *target*):
one note follows another, a mark is attached to a note,
a part performs a line.
Every edge has a kind, an identifier, a source, a target, metadata,
and the fields its kind defines.

A **value** is an immutable piece of musical data with no identity of its own:
a pitch, a duration, a time signature, a staccato.
Two values with the same type and the same fields are the same value.
Values are the fields of nodes, of edges, and of other values.

**Identity.** Every node and every edge has an identifier, a UUID,
that stays with it for as long as it exists, in every document it is written to.
Values have no identifiers.

**Metadata** (`@meta`, and the graph's `info`)
is free-form data that applications attach to a node, an edge or the graph:
an editor's on-screen placement of a note, an importer's record of its source.
It is not interpreted by OMK, and this specification says nothing about its content
beyond the rules of §4.9.

## 4. Primitive types

The vocabularies give each field one of the following types.
A type written with a trailing `?` (`string?`) also admits `null`.

### 4.1 `string`, `boolean`, `null`

As in JSON.
A string MUST NOT contain a lone surrogate code point.

### 4.2 `integer`

A JSON number with no fraction and no exponent.
Readers MUST preserve integers exactly, whatever their size.

### 4.3 `rational`

An exact rational number.
A whole number is written as an `integer`;
any other value is written as a string `"n/d"`:
the numerator `n` (with a leading `-` if negative) and the denominator `d`,
in lowest terms, with `d` greater than 1,
and no spaces, no leading zeros and no `+` sign.

```json
3        "1/2"       "-7/3"       0
```

A rational MUST NOT be written as a JSON number with a fraction or an exponent.
The format never uses floating-point numbers for musical data.

### 4.4 `uuid`

A UUID ([RFC 9562](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9562)) as a string
of 36 characters in the hyphenated form, with lowercase hexadecimal digits:
`"5d1e7a40-3c2b-4f6e-9a8d-0b1c2d3e4f50"`.
Any UUID version is permitted.

### 4.5 Enumerations

A string drawn from a list given by a vocabulary.
Enumeration values are case-sensitive and are written exactly as listed.
Every enumeration value is an identifier in lowercase `snake_case`
(`"articulation"`, `"rim_shot"`, `"low_mid"`):
never containing spaces, hyphens or capitals.

### 4.6 `array<T>`

A JSON array whose elements are of type `T`, in order.
Order is significant.

### 4.7 `set<T>`

A JSON array whose elements are of type `T`, all distinct, in no significant order.
Writers MUST write the elements in canonical order (§9.5);
readers MUST NOT give the order any meaning,
and MUST reject a set holding two equal elements.

### 4.8 System identifiers

A string naming a tonal or temporal system, as declared by a vocabulary (§6.4).

### 4.9 `json`

Any JSON value, subject to these rules:

- object keys MUST be unique within each object;
- a number with a fraction or an exponent MUST be finite
  and is written in canonical form (§9.3);
- strings follow §4.1.

`json` is used only for metadata (`@meta` and the graph's `info`).

As in JSON itself, a number in `json` data is just a number:
the format does not record whether it was an integer or a floating-point value.
A number written without a fraction or an exponent reads back as an integer,
and the canonical form (§9.3) writes a whole-valued float that way (`100.0` is written `100`).
For a float of magnitude 2^53 or more, the integer its canonical text spells
is its shortest round-tripping spelling, which need not be its exact value.

### 4.10 Tagged values

Every value that is not a primitive is a JSON object with a key `@type`,
whose string names the value's type (§7.1),
and one key for each field that type defines.
Where a field may hold values of several types
(a duration may be a metrical duration, a clock duration, a tied duration, ...),
the vocabularies name a *kind* (§7.3), and `@type` says which type the value is.

## 5. The document

A document is a single JSON object with exactly these keys:

| key | type | content |
|---|---|---|
| `format` | string | the literal `"omk-json"` |
| `vocabularies` | object | the vocabularies the document uses (§6) |
| `graph` | object | the graph's metadata (§5.1) |
| `nodes` | `array` of node objects | §8.1 |
| `edges` | `array` of edge objects | §8.2 |

### 5.1 The graph's metadata

An object with exactly these keys:

| key | type | |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | `string?` | a name for the graph as a container |
| `description` | `string?` | |
| `info` | object of `json` | free-form metadata about the graph (§3) |

The metadata of a *work* (title, composer, ...) is not here:
it is on a `Score` node,
because a graph may hold several works, or fragments that are none.

## 6. Vocabularies

A vocabulary is a published, versioned set of names:
node types, edge kinds, value types, kinds, enumerations,
edge relations, and system identifiers.
This version of the format defines two:
[`omk`](vocabulary-omk.qmd), the core, which every document uses,
and [`wsmn`](vocabulary-wsmn.qmd), Western Standard Music Notation.
Extensions define their own.

### 6.1 Identification

A vocabulary is identified by a URI.
The URI is an identifier only; it need not resolve.

| vocabulary | URI | preferred prefix |
|---|---|---|
| core | `https://openmusickit.org/spec/omk` | `omk` |
| Western Standard Music Notation | `https://openmusickit.org/spec/wsmn` | `wsmn` |

### 6.2 The `vocabularies` object

The `vocabularies` object maps a *prefix* to an object with exactly two keys,
`uri` (a string) and `version` (a string, §6.3):

```json
"vocabularies": {
  "omk": {"uri": "https://openmusickit.org/spec/omk", "version": "0.1"},
  "wsmn": {"uri": "https://openmusickit.org/spec/wsmn", "version": "0.1"}
}
```

A prefix is a string of lowercase ASCII letters, digits and hyphens,
beginning with a letter.
Prefixes are local to the document:
a reader identifies a vocabulary by its `uri`, never by its prefix.
The same URI MUST NOT appear under two prefixes.

The `omk` vocabulary MUST be present, under the prefix `omk`.
Its names are written without a prefix (§7.1).

The object MUST list exactly the vocabularies whose names appear in the document,
plus `omk`.
A writer uses each vocabulary's preferred prefix.

This object is the document's list of requirements:
a reader that does not implement every vocabulary listed,
at a version it supports, MUST refuse the document (§10).

### 6.3 Versions

A version is a string `"major.minor"` of two non-negative integers
with no leading zeros.
A reader that implements version *M.n* of a vocabulary
MUST accept a document requiring version *M.m* of it when *m* ≤ *n*, and *M* ≥ 1;
while *M* is 0, it MUST accept only *0.n* exactly.
It MUST refuse every other version.

Within a major version (from 1 onwards), a new minor version only adds:
new types, kinds, fields of new types, enumeration values, relations, or systems.
It never changes or removes what an earlier minor version defined.

### 6.4 System identifiers

A tonal or temporal *system* is a musical system that values belong to:
WSMN's metrical time, clock time, WSMN's pitch system.
Most values imply their system by their type
(a `wsmn:MetricalDuration` is in WSMN's metrical time),
so systems appear in documents only where a node names one directly
(`SyncLine.temporal_system`).

Each vocabulary declares identifiers for its systems.
Tonal and temporal systems are separate namespaces,
since a field's type always says which is meant.
Identifiers follow the same prefix rule as type names (§7.1).

## 7. Names

### 7.1 Qualified names

A name defined by the `omk` vocabulary is written bare: `NoteEvent`, `ClockDuration`, `marks`.
A name defined by any other vocabulary is written `prefix:Name`,
where `prefix` is that vocabulary's prefix in the `vocabularies` object:
`wsmn:TonalVector`, `wsmn:metrical`.

This applies to `@type` values, edge relations, and system identifiers.
It does not apply to field names or enumeration values,
which belong to the type that defines them.

### 7.2 Type names and field names

Each vocabulary defines its types, and for each type its fields:
a name, a primitive type or kind, whether `null` is admitted,
and the field's domain (the values it may take).
Field names are written as defined, in `snake_case`.

### 7.3 Kinds

A *kind* names a set of types that may appear in the same field:
`Duration`, `Tone`, `Measurable`, ...
A vocabulary defines kinds and says which of its own types belong to which kinds;
a later vocabulary may add its own types to an earlier vocabulary's kinds.
(An extension's new duration type belongs to the kind `Duration`,
and may then appear wherever a duration may.)

## 8. Nodes and edges

### 8.1 Node objects

A node is a JSON object with these keys, and no others:

| key | type | |
|---|---|---|
| `@id` | `uuid` | the node's identifier |
| `@type` | string | the node's type: a node type of some vocabulary |
| `@meta` | object of `json` | the node's metadata (§3) |
| *field* | as defined | one key for each field of the type (§8.3) |

### 8.2 Edge objects

An edge is a JSON object with these keys, and no others:

| key | type | |
|---|---|---|
| `@id` | `uuid` | the edge's identifier |
| `@type` | string | the edge's kind: an edge kind of some vocabulary |
| `@source` | `uuid` | the `@id` of the edge's source node |
| `@target` | `uuid` | the `@id` of the edge's target node |
| `@meta` | object of `json` | the edge's metadata (§3) |
| *field* | as defined | one key for each field of the kind (§8.3) |

The core edge kinds (`Next`, `Branch`, `Simultaneous`, `Contains`, `Edge`)
and the core relations are defined by the [`omk` vocabulary](vocabulary-omk.qmd#edges).
Every edge has a *relation*, the kind of relationship it asserts:
for `Edge` it is the field `relation`;
for the other kinds it is implied by the kind.

### 8.3 Fields

Every field the type defines MUST be present,
including fields whose value is `null`
and fields whose value is what an implementation might consider a default.
No other keys are permitted.
(So the content of a document never depends on any implementation's defaults.)

Keys beginning with `@` are reserved for this specification;
no vocabulary defines a field whose name begins with `@`.

## 9. Canonical form

Every graph has exactly one canonical document.
Writers MUST produce it.
Readers MUST accept any document that is valid JSON
and otherwise conforms to this specification, canonical or not.

### 9.1 Encoding

UTF-8, with no byte order mark.
Lines end with a single LF (U+000A).
The document ends with a single LF.

### 9.2 Layout

- Each object key is followed by `": "` (a colon and one space).
- The members of an object, and the elements of an array,
  are each written on their own line,
  indented two spaces more than the line that opened the object or array,
  and separated by a comma at the end of each line except the last.
  The closing `}` or `]` is on its own line,
  at the indentation of the line that opened it.
- An empty object is written `{}`, and an empty array `[]`.
- There is no other whitespace.

This is the layout that, for example, Python's
`json.dumps(value, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)`
and JavaScript's `JSON.stringify(value, null, 2)` produce,
apart from the key order (§9.4) and the number and string rules (§9.3).

### 9.3 Strings and numbers

Strings and numbers are serialised as
[RFC 8785](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8785) (JSON Canonicalization Scheme) §3.2.2 specifies.
In short:

- a string escapes `"` as `\"`, `\` as `\\`,
  the control characters U+0008, U+0009, U+000A, U+000C and U+000D
  as `\b`, `\t`, `\n`, `\f` and `\r`,
  and every other control character below U+0020 as `\u` followed by four lowercase hexadecimal digits;
  no other character is escaped;
- an integer is written in decimal, with a `-` if negative, and no leading zeros;
- a number with a fraction (only possible in `json` data, §4.9)
  is written as ECMAScript's `Number.prototype.toString` writes it
  (the shortest form that reads back as the same IEEE 754 double).

### 9.4 Order

- The keys of every object are sorted by Unicode code point.
  (So `@`-keys come before all field names.)
- The elements of `nodes` and of `edges` are sorted by `@id`.
- The elements of a `set` are sorted as §9.5 says.
- Every other array keeps its own order.

Sorting nodes and edges by `@id` is defined for every graph, however incomplete,
and is stable under edits: adding a note adds one block to a textual diff.

### 9.5 The order of a set

The elements of a `set` are sorted by their canonical serialisation
as a sequence of Unicode code points,
each element serialised on its own as §9.1–9.4 describe, starting at indentation zero.

## 10. Readers

A reader MUST refuse a document, and add nothing to any graph, if:

- it is not valid JSON, or an object in it has two equal keys;
- its `format` is not `"omk-json"`,
  or the document, or any node, edge, value or envelope object,
  has a key this specification does not allow there, or lacks one it requires;
- `vocabularies` lacks `omk` (under the prefix `omk`),
  lists a URI twice,
  or lists a vocabulary the reader does not implement at a version it accepts (§6.3);
  the reader SHOULD name every such vocabulary, with its URI and version,
  so that a user can tell what is missing;
- a qualified name uses a prefix not listed in `vocabularies`,
  or names a type, relation or system that its vocabulary does not define;
- a value has the wrong type for its field
  (including a value whose `@type` is not of the field's kind),
  or lies outside the field's domain,
  even where an implementation's own constructors would accept it;
- any two nodes or edges (two nodes, two edges, or a node and an edge) have the same `@id`,
  or an edge's `@source` or `@target` is not the `@id` of a node in the document;
- two edges have the same source, target and relation;
- two edges with relation `next` have the same source,
  or two have the same target.

A reader MUST NOT refuse a document for musical incompleteness:
a note with no duration, a line with no part, a graph with no score.
The rules above are all the structure a graph is required to have.

A reader that adds a document to a graph that already holds nodes or edges
MUST refuse it if any `@id` in the document is already in the graph.
It MUST NOT change the existing graph's own metadata.

## 11. Writers

A writer MUST write the canonical form (§9).
It MUST refuse to write a graph that holds:

- a node, an edge or a value of a type that no vocabulary it implements defines,
  including a specialisation of a defined type whose own type is not defined;
- a value outside its field's domain;
- a system that no vocabulary declares;
- metadata that is not `json` (§4.9).

## 12. Round trips

For a reader and writer that conform to this specification:

- **document → graph → document.**
  Reading a canonical document and writing the graph produces the same bytes.
- **graph → document → graph.**
  Writing a graph and reading the document produces a graph with
  the same node and edge identifiers,
  every edge between the same nodes,
  every node, edge and value of the same type with the same fields,
  and the same metadata.

What an implementation holds and the format does not carry:

- the distinction between an integer and a whole-number rational
  (`2` and `2/1` are the same number, and are written `2`);
- in metadata, the distinction between an integer and a whole-valued float (§4.9);
- whether two nodes share one value object or hold equal copies
  (values have no identity, §3);
- anything about how the graph is stored.

## 13. Examples

One middle-C quarter note with a staccato dot, in a graph named "Sketch"
([`examples/sketch.omk.json`](examples/sketch.omk.json)):

```json
{
  "edges": [
    {
      "@id": "78e51061-7311-48a3-82ce-6f447ed4d57b",
      "@meta": {},
      "@source": "1e2feb89-414c-443c-9027-c4d1c386bbc4",
      "@target": "cd613e30-d8f1-4adf-91b7-584a2265b1f5",
      "@type": "Edge",
      "origin": "asserted",
      "relation": "marks"
    }
  ],
  "format": "omk-json",
  "graph": {
    "description": null,
    "info": {},
    "name": "Sketch"
  },
  "nodes": [
    {
      "@id": "1e2feb89-414c-443c-9027-c4d1c386bbc4",
      "@meta": {},
      "@type": "Marking",
      "mark": {
        "@type": "Mark",
        "aliases": [],
        "attachment_mode": "single",
        "binds": false,
        "description": "A staccato dot: the note is played detached and shortened.",
        "kind": "articulation",
        "name": "staccato"
      }
    },
    {
      "@id": "cd613e30-d8f1-4adf-91b7-584a2265b1f5",
      "@meta": {},
      "@type": "NoteEvent",
      "duration": {
        "@type": "wsmn:MetricalDuration",
        "denominator": 4,
        "dots": 0,
        "numerator": 1,
        "ratio": null
      },
      "tones": [
        {
          "@type": "wsmn:TonalVector",
          "chromatic": 0,
          "diatonic": 0,
          "octave": 0
        }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "vocabularies": {
    "omk": {
      "uri": "https://openmusickit.org/spec/omk",
      "version": "0.1"
    },
    "wsmn": {
      "uri": "https://openmusickit.org/spec/wsmn",
      "version": "0.1"
    }
  }
}
```

A fuller fragment, [`examples/fragment.omk.json`](examples/fragment.omk.json),
has a scored line under a slur, a second voice branched off it,
a sung syllable, an editor's metadata, and a note pinned to a film's clock.

Both are written by the reference implementation, and its tests check
that they read back and write the same bytes, and that this page shows the first of them exactly.
